Reserves

Does a DC condo association need a reserve study?

For Washington, DC condo boards · Updated November 14, 2026

The short answer

DC law does not require a reserve study or a minimum reserve balance. The DC Condominium Act lets the board adopt a budget that includes reserves (§ 42-1903.08), and your declaration or bylaws may require more. Most buildings still need one: buyers see your reserves on every resale certificate, and mortgage lenders look at reserve funding before they lend in the building.

What DC law says about reserves

  • The board may budget for reserves. The association has the power to adopt and amend a budget for revenues, expenditures and reserves, and to collect assessments for common expenses (§ 42-1903.08).
  • Board members owe owners a fiduciary's care. The same section says officers and executive board members must exercise the care required of a fiduciary of the unit owners.
  • Assessments are made at least once a year, or more often if the condominium instruments say so (§ 42-1903.12).
  • Reserves are disclosed on every resale. The seller must give the buyer a statement of the status and amount of any reserves for capital expenditures, contingencies and improvements, any part earmarked for a specific project, and any approved capital expenditures not in the current operating budget (§ 42-1904.11).

Nothing in the Act sets a required reserve balance or says how often to study it. That makes your own documents the deciding rules.

Check your declaration and bylaws

Many DC condominium instruments are stricter than the Act. Look for language that requires a reserve fund, a minimum yearly contribution, or a reserve study on a set schedule. If your documents require it, the board must follow them.

Why boards get a reserve study anyway

  • Sales. Buyers and their agents read the reserve figures on the resale certificate. A thin reserve with a roof due soon is a reason to walk away or ask for a lower price.
  • Mortgages. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac review a building's budget before lenders sell loans to them, and a budget that sets too little aside for reserves can make units harder to finance. The commonly cited benchmark is 10% of the budget going to reserves.
  • Special assessments. Without a plan, a boiler or façade repair becomes a large one-time bill for every owner.
  • Fiduciary care. A study is the clearest record that the board planned for what it knew was coming.

What a reserve study covers

A reserve study lists every major shared component, such as the roof, boiler, elevator, façade, windows, paving and common-area finishes, with its remaining useful life and replacement cost. It then sets a yearly contribution that pays for each one when it comes due. Common practice is a full study with a site visit, then updates every few years; many boards use a three to five year cycle.

Checklist for a self-managed board

  1. Read the declaration and bylaws for any reserve rules.
  2. List every shared component with the year it was installed or last replaced.
  3. Commission a reserve study, or an update if the last one is more than a few years old.
  4. Set the reserve contribution in the annual budget and send the budget to owners.
  5. Move the reserve contribution to a separate account every month.
  6. Keep the study in the association's records; you will need it for every resale certificate.
